content: Clinical data from the ACTG protocol 076 study demonstrated that ZDV was effective in preventing perinatal transmission of HIV, even in cases where genotypic evidence of maternal ZDV resistance was present. Therefore, based on the available evidence, ZDV remains a reasonable first-line choice for PEP regimens. There is no direct evidence to support the addition of other antiretroviral drugs to ZDV to enhance the efficacy of PEP. However, in HIV-infected patients, combination antiretroviral regimens have been shown to be more effective than monotherapy in reducing viral load. The decision regarding which agents to use, how many to include, or when to modify a PEP regimen is largely empirical. Guidelines for early HIV infection treatment recommend the use of three drugs (two NRTIs and a PI), but the applicability of these recommendations to PEP remains uncertain. NRTIs that can be considered for use with ZDV in PEP include lamivudine (3TC), didanosine (ddI), and zalcitabine. These agents have been included in recommended regimens that incorporate ZDV. Previous CDC recommendations identified 3TC as a preferred second agent for PEP due to the enhanced antiretroviral activity of the ZDV/3TC combination, its efficacy against many ZDV-resistant HIV strains, and its lack of substantial additional toxicity. Furthermore, data suggest that ZDV-resistant mutations develop more slowly in patients receiving the ZDV/3TC combination compared to ZDV alone. In vitro studies also indicate that the mutation associated with 3TC resistance may reverse ZDV phenotypic resistance. No new information has emerged to alter the original recommendation of 3TC as the second agent for PEP. Additionally, the availability of a combination formulation of ZDV and 3TC (Combivir™) may make 3TC a more convenient option for healthcare workers (HCWs). However, individual clinicians may prefer other NRTIs or combinations of antiretroviral agents based on local knowledge and experience in treating HIV infection and disease. Previously, indinavir (IDV) was recommended as the PI of choice for PEP due to its higher bioavailability compared to saquinavir and its more favorable immediate toxicity profile compared to ritonavir. Additionally, the need for dose escalation when initiating ritonavir makes it less practical for PEP use. Since the 1996 PEP recommendations, nelfinavir (NEL) has been approved by the FDA and is now included in regimens recommended for the treatment of primary HIV infection. The FDA has also recently approved a soft-gel formulation of saquinavir (Fortovase™) with improved bioavailability compared to its hard-gel formulation (Invirase™). However, the recommended dose of soft-gel saquinavir (1200 mg three times daily) is double that of the hard-gel formulation (600 mg three times daily) and requires taking 18 pills per day, which may affect HCW compliance if used for PEP. Based on these considerations, either IDV or NEL is recommended as the first choice for inclusion in an expanded PEP regimen. If saquinavir is preferred by the prescribing physician, the soft-gel formulation (Fortovase™) should be used. Differences in the side effects associated with IDV and NEL may also influence the choice of agent in specific situations. Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs), such as nevirapine and delavirdine, have not been included in the recommended PEP regimens. As a class, NNRTIs are fast-acting and potent, making them conceptually appealing for PEP. Additionally, there is some evidence of prophylactic efficacy. However, concerns about side effects and the availability of alternative agents argue against routinely using this class of drugs for initial PEP. With expert consultation, an NNRTI might be considered in specific cases. An important goal of PEP is to encourage and facilitate compliance with a four-week regimen. Therefore, the toxicity profile of antiretroviral agents, including the frequency, severity, duration, and reversibility of side effects, is a relevant consideration. All antiretroviral agents have been associated with side effects, although studies of adverse events have primarily been conducted in individuals with advanced disease and longer treatment courses, which may not reflect the experience of those with less advanced disease or uninfected individuals. Side effects associated with many NRTIs, such as ZDV or ddI, are primarily gastrointestinal (e.g., nausea or diarrhea), and the incidence of adverse effects has generally not been greater when these agents are used in combination. All approved PIs may have potentially serious drug interactions when used with certain other medications, requiring careful evaluation of concomitant medications being used by an HCW before prescribing a PI and close monitoring for toxicity during PEP. PIs may inhibit the metabolism of non-sedating antihistamines and other hepatically metabolized drugs. The use of PIs has also been associated with new-onset diabetes mellitus, hyperglycemia, diabetic ketoacidosis, and exacerbation of pre-existing diabetes mellitus. Nephrolithiasis has been associated with IDV use, including in HCWs using the drug for PEP; however, the incidence of this complication may be limited by adequate hydration (e.g., drinking at least 48 oz or 1.5 L of fluid per 24-hour period). Rare cases of hemolytic anemia have also been associated with IDV use. NEL, saquinavir, and ritonavir have been associated with the development of diarrhea, which usually responds to treatment with antimotility agents that can be prescribed at the time these drugs are initiated for PEP.
